en: The stranger’s affairs prospered,
And the man who fought him vanished.
Such was Külchoro’s nature.
Unable to endure his fury,
He confronted his bloodthirsty lord;
The poor soul could not contain himself,
His heart burned and became flame.
Coiling like a venomous snake,
The warrior Choro, the gray-maned lion, grew fierce;
His heart burned into embers—
How could he possibly stand still?
Burning and blazing, he turned sideways,
And the noble Choro began to speak:
“You were a heroic, gray-maned lord,
The mighty protector on whom I relied.
No foe could overcome your snowy heights,
No enemy could advance against you.
You were a towering black mountain pass,
And I was the one who took shelter in you.
Hero, you were orphaned of your father,
You grew to manhood as an orphan,
And barely rejoined your people.
When you reached twelve years of age,
You became a blazing ember,
A leaping red flame.
You shattered royal camps and took their spoils,
And attacked mighty nations.
Sated with blood, you grew fierce,
And were named the bloodthirsty gray-maned lion.
You enriched the people of the valleys;
When those you hated fell into your hands,
You laid Khan Jakyp low.
You sent Köbösh into the grave
And revealed your gray-maned valor.
You conquered the Sary-Kaikan pass,
And seized every land your heart desired.
Hero, though I implored you, you ignored my words
And brought me to this wretched state.
My words sweeter than sugar—
You sought to break my back.
You passed through me like consuming fire;
From time to time,
You sought to blind my eyes.
Alas, my lord, you have not prospered;
You brought disgrace and humiliated me.
My heart sinks and I am torn apart:
If I call you alive, you are not among the living;
If I call you dead, you are not in the grave—
Why did you appear before my eyes?
You burned me until I was seared,
Blackened me into a coal,
And destroyed my precious life.
You revealed your mighty valor;
Without smoke and without flame,
You set me smoldering and burned me.
You began this grievous affliction.
On the uplands, the horses are piebald,
Thoroughbreds mingled with stallions;
You abandoned your livestock.
Fashioned with a shaft of gold,
You abandoned your throne.
Your speech is sweet and your words are honey;
Bloodthirsty lord, hear me without causing grief.
Do not loosen my shovel-like teeth,
Do not burn my heart like this.
Do not boil and burn into embers
The man who looked to you for protection.
I mourned and searched for many years;
Now that what I lost has been found,
How can I keep from dissolving,
When I have encountered my tiger, my elder brother?
My precious elder brother, begin to speak;
Lay aside your lordly pride.
Now I shall die at your hands—
The true realm from which none returns,
By the power of almighty Khidr-Allah.
Through twelve rearguards and forty scouts,
I offered my breast to bullets.
You made me suffer boundless affliction
And endure dreadful humiliation.
Famed Keng-Shor and Kan-Jailak,
Ülgülüü-Maral and Kümüsh-Tak,
The banks of Besh-Tash and Kapka-Tash—
You abandoned these lands.
The dependent Kyrgyz and the many Argyn—
You abandoned your people.
O great plane tree with lofty branches,
You abandoned your fruit.
Until the five-argali constellation had set,
She widened her womb five times,
She opened her constricted belly
And let down milk from her stony breast—
You abandoned your mother.
Your father’s confidant,
The noble Bakai, his companion,
Blessed in his old age—
You abandoned your forefather.
Six months in the womb, the ill-fated one—
Hero, you abandoned your child.
Reedy Keng-Kol and broad Talas,
The many Kyrgyz encamped in rows,
Kumiss by day and maidens by night—
You abandoned your homeland.
The moonlike woman Aichürök—
You abandoned your wife.
Argali on your hills, wild asses on your plains—
You abandoned your land.
Placed before you, I was a blessed path;
Sent into battle, I was like a countless host.
You abandoned me.
Though I implored you, you ignored my words;
You bent my wretched back,
Spread your unbreakable net,
And showed me great suffering.
You had Kanchoro strip from you
Your flowered robe that no bullet could pierce.
My ancestral home is mighty Kakanchyn;
My anger has risen and I stand enraged.
Bloodthirsty warrior, I shall slaughter you—
How could I leave you alive?
Lest people say that mighty Semetey,
Whose support was like iron,
Had become mute;
Lest people say the bloodthirsty lion,
Once the just one, had become witless;
Lest, because he speaks no words and utters no speech,
They say that he has gone mad—
If I do not truly gouge out your eyes,
If I do not slaughter you, my true lord!
I endured hellish torment like this;
I endured so much grief for you—
Alas, my lord, if I do not slaughter you!
May the heavens strike me before I can cry “Ah,”
And may the spirit of my father Manas
Strike me squarely upon the crown.
May the sealed blue sky strike me,
May the broad-breasted earth strike me,
May the spark of the white matchlock strike me,
May the bullet of the white musket strike me.
My lord, I shall slaughter you
And put an end to you.
My anger rising as I stand enraged,
I shall take keen steel in hand;
My mighty elder brother, brave gray-maned lion,
I shall bring calamity upon you.
I have endured so much torment because of you.
If I do not slaughter you, my elder brother,
If I do not put an end to you!
I shall throw the people below into tumult
And delight every soul who hears:
‘My mighty elder brother has died,’
‘The dear man has gone
To the true realm from which none returns.’
Every army will gather in a throng,
And dust will soar into the sky.
‘My mighty elder brother has died,’ they will say;
If it falls upon my head, I shall see.
I shall spill my noble blood,
Valuing it no more than a fly;
In truth I shall sacrifice
My golden life, slight as a fly.
Though I implore you, you will not speak;
Though I speak again, my brother, you will not mend.
You twist and struggle to flee like a spirit,
Preparing your way of escape.
Broad, level Sary-Adyrmak,
The people’s autumn pasture beneath the hail—
I have no livestock left to drive there.
My own elder brother has become my enemy;
I have no life I would spare from death.
I sing my song in earnest,
And strengthen my powerful resolve;
Do not call forth my infidel wrath.
The reason I spare you not is true:
When I was about to die,
I was a slave in a sheepskin;
While I remained alive,
I was the son of a dogskin slave.
I am one who has tightly girded his waist;
I know well where
You and I were born together,
Sharing every affliction.
My dear mother Kanykei—
We kicked our way out, wounding her womb.
Great Manas, towering like a cliff—
We sprang from his mighty loins.
We entered one delight together,
Grew together and lay in blood,
And lay within a single womb—
When was I ever a son of Manas?
If called a slave, then a slave I am;
From this surging host of Kakan,
I was the son of your wretched elder brother.
My first father was Chylaba,
My ancestral city is Bakburchun,
My lineage is the Chinese of Chynmachyn.
Without speaking a word or uttering a sound,
You cast embers into my fleshly heart.
You brought great suffering upon my soul,
You drained away much of my strength,
You seared my soul again and again,
You utterly chilled my breath,
You broke my back.
Again you did a wondrous thing,
Setting my very core aflame,
You sought to make my misery boil,
Uncle, I shall die by your hand,
I shall not let you go unless I die.
If I do not see your true resting place,
If I do not die together with you,
If I do not hew off his head with an axe,
If I do not cut through his neck with a sword,
If I do not see the face of the world beyond,
If I do not die locked in your embrace,
May I die unworthy of the name Külchoro,
Let me see whether you will speak.
Just utter something by chance,
And I shall take it as a sign.
If you will not speak to me,
If you will not heed what I say,
I shall disfigure you now,
I shall unleash my towering rage.
I said I had fallen into the embers for you,
I was scorched and became an ember myself.
I burned and burned until I was gone,
I wore out my heroic head,
I aged my strongman's soul.
I was blinded and became as a grave,
I became level with the black earth.
Every ordeal and mighty torment,
I was the one who endured it all.
For you, bloodthirsty villain of the dark day,
Only a spoonful of my blood remains,
My flesh is left bruised and raw,
I fell from my course and was left bereft.
When the mighty gray-maned hero was lost,
They said, “The valiant man has seen
The true abode from which none return,”
They would wash him with koumiss,
And wrap him in brocade,
They would wash him with Zamzam water,
And bind him in cloth of gold,
Entrust him to the wise for safekeeping,
And have singers praise him,
Entrust him to men of honor,
And have poets sing his praise.
If I do not bury him with my own hands,
May I die unworthy of the name Külchoro,
May I sink into darkness as though never born.
Turn your neck toward me,
Uncle, while you are still alive,
Reveal your inmost secret.
The song you spoke in truth,
Speak it sincerely as your creed.
Tell me the secret within you,
Tell me the truth.
